reasoning.Student A:
The mechanism's key property says the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my "Obtainable Schools") is fixed given others' rankings and school priorities, and my own ranking cannot change which schools are in that set. My ranking only determines which school I get within that fixed set — I receive the highest-ranked school (in my list) that lies in the Obtainable Schools.

Therefore the optimal strategy is simply to rank sincerely: put my true most-preferred school first, then second-most, etc. Manipulating the order cannot make an unattainable school become attainable, so there is no benefit to misrepresenting preferences.

Given my stated preferences x > w > z > y (and noting my priorities: w:1, x:2, y:1, z:2, and that most others favor y > x > w > z), I should list schools in my true preference order. If the Obtainable Schools include multiple options, I will receive the highest-ranked among them — which is maximized by ranking truthfully.

Because the mechanism fixes the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my "Obtainable Schools") based on others' rankings and priorities, my submitted ranking cannot change which schools are obtainable for me. It only chooses which obtainable school I receive by picking the highest-ranked among them.

Given my true preferences (x > w > z > y) and the priorities (I have priority 1 at x and z, priority 2 at w and y), the correct strategy is to rank schools in my true preference order. I should not try to "hedge" by promoting a safer school (e.g., z) above a more-preferred school (w) because doing so cannot expand the set of obtainable schools — it only picks among that fixed set. If w is in my obtainable set, I want it above z; if it is not, ranking it higher won't make it obtainable. Also, y is widely favored by others and I have lower priority there, so listing y higher would not improve my chances of getting it if it's not in my obtainable set.

Therefore I submit my true preference order.

Because of that, there is no benefit to misranking a more-preferred obtainable school below a less-preferred obtainable school: doing so could only make me end up at a less-preferred school within the same obtainable set. Therefore I should rank schools in true preference order.

Practical considerations that reinforce truth-telling here:
- My stated preferences are z > x > w > y.
- Most other applicants favor y first, so y is likely to be oversubscribed; my priority at y (3) is not especially high, so y is unlikely to be in my obtainable set anyway. That makes ranking y last sensible.
- I have equal priority (3) at z and y but demand patterns make z more attainable; since I most prefer z, it should be top.
Thus I will submit my true ranking: z > x > w > y.
